result:
CORS is browser-only rule. curl does not enforce it.

Browser blocks page JavaScript from reading a cross-origin response unless server sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` matching page origin. Server often still receives and answers the request; browser withholds the response. curl has no origin and no same-origin policy, so it shows whatever comes back.

Second cause: preflight. For non-simple requests (custom headers like `Authorization`, `Content-Type: application/json`, methods like `PUT`/`DELETE`), browser first sends `OPTIONS`. If server answers that without right `Access-Control-Allow-*` headers, real request never goes. curl skips preflight.

Reproduce in curl:

```
curl -i -X OPTIONS https://api.example.com/path \
  -H "Origin: https://your-site.com" \
  -H "Access-Control-Request-Method: POST" \
  -H "Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type, authorization"
```

Check response for `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`, `Access-Control-Allow-Headers`. Missing or mismatched means that is the block.

Fix on server, not client: return those headers for your origin and handle `OPTIONS`. With cookies/credentials, `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` must be exact origin, not `*`, plus `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. No control of server? Route through same-origin proxy on your backend.
